rva = pl.read_csv(ub + "data/flightsrva_flights.csv.gz", null_values=["NA"])
airline = pl.read_csv(ub + "data/flightsrva_airlines.csv.gz", null_values=["NA"])
airport = pl.read_csv(ub + "data/flightsrva_airports.csv.gz", null_values=["NA"])
plane = pl.read_csv(ub + "data/flightsrva_planes.csv.gz", null_values=["NA"])

### Questions

Five tables this time. `rva` has one row for each of the 24,808 commercial flights
that left Richmond International Airport in 2019, with the date, the scheduled and
actual times, the delays in minutes, the `carrier` code of the airline, the `tailnum`
of the aircraft, and the `dest` code of the airport it flew to.

The other four tables describe things that the flights point to. `airline` has one
row per airline, with the two-letter `carrier` code and the airline's `name`.
`airport` has one row per airport, with its three-letter `faa` code, `name`, `lat`,
and `lon`. `plane` has one row per aircraft, with its `tailnum`, the `year` it was
built, and the number of `seats`. `weather` has one row per hour of the year, with
`year`, `month`, `day`, `hour`, the `wind_speed`, and the visibility `visib` in miles.

Unless a question says otherwise, just print the result of each block; do not save it
to a variable.

1. Start with one table. Count the number of flights for each `carrier` and sort from
the most flights to the fewest.

```{python}
(
    rva
    .group_by(c.carrier)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .sort(c.n, descending=True)
)
```

There are 14 carriers. The codes are hard to read: who are `OO` and `9E`?

2. Compute the mean departure delay (`dep_delay`) for each `month`, sort by month, and
draw it as a line plot.

```{python}
(
    rva
    .group_by(c.month)
    .agg(mean_dep_delay = c.dep_delay.mean())
    .sort(c.month)
    .ggplot(aes(c.month, c.mean_dep_delay))
    .geom_line()
)
```

June and July are the worst months, at around 15 minutes late on average.

3. Join `airline` onto `rva` using the key `carrier`, and select the columns `carrier`,
`name`, and `dest`.

```{python}
(
    rva
    .join(airline, on=c.carrier)
    .select(c.carrier, c.name, c.dest)
)
```

The result still has 24,808 rows, one per flight. Each flight now carries the full
name of its airline.

4. Take the code from the previous question, but instead of selecting columns, group
by `name` and compute the number of flights and the mean departure delay. Sort from
the largest mean delay to the smallest.

```{python}
(
    rva
    .join(airline, on=c.carrier)
    .group_by(c.name)
    .agg(
        n = pl.len(),
        mean_dep_delay = c.dep_delay.mean()
    )
    .sort(c.mean_dep_delay, descending=True)
)
```

ExpressJet is the worst at 23 minutes late on average. Delta is the best at under two
minutes.

5. Now the destinations. Count the number of flights to each `dest`, then join
`airport` to get the airport names. The key has a different name in the two tables,
`dest` in the flights and `faa` in the airports, so use `left_on` and `right_on`. Sort
by the number of flights.

```{python}
(
    rva
    .group_by(c.dest)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .join(airport, left_on=c.dest, right_on=c.faa)
    .sort(c.n, descending=True)
)
```

Richmond flies to 22 airports. Atlanta is by far the most common destination.

6. Take the code from the previous question and draw a map: longitude on the x-axis,
latitude on the y-axis, and the size of each point given by the number of flights.

```{python}
(
    rva
    .group_by(c.dest)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .join(airport, left_on=c.dest, right_on=c.faa)
    .ggplot(aes(c.lon, c.lat))
    .geom_point(aes(size=c.n))
)
```

The flights table had no coordinates in it. The join brought them in from `airport`.

7. Join `plane` onto `rva` using the key `tailnum`. Then group by `carrier` and compute
the number of flights and the mean number of `seats`. Sort by the mean number of seats.

```{python}
(
    rva
    .join(plane, on=c.tailnum)
    .group_by(c.carrier)
    .agg(
        n = pl.len(),
        mean_seats = c.seats.mean()
    )
    .sort(c.mean_seats, descending=True)
)
```

Count the rows: there are only 13 carriers here, not 14. One airline has disappeared,
and Polars did not give any warning.

8. Find out what happened with an anti-join. Keep the flights in `rva` that have no
matching `tailnum` in `plane`, and count them by `carrier`.

```{python}
(
    rva
    .join(plane, on=c.tailnum, how="anti")
    .group_by(c.carrier)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .sort(c.n, descending=True)
)
```

All 396 flights by `G4` (Allegiant Air) are missing from the `plane` table. The default
inner join dropped every one of them.

9. Go back to the code from question 7 and make it a left join. Allegiant should come
back, with a missing value for the mean number of seats.

```{python}
(
    rva
    .join(plane, on=c.tailnum, how="left")
    .group_by(c.carrier)
    .agg(
        n = pl.len(),
        mean_seats = c.seats.mean()
    )
    .sort(c.mean_seats, descending=True)
)
```

A left join keeps every row of the left table, so all 14 carriers are back. Allegiant
is printed first because a sort puts missing values at the top. We know that Allegiant
flew 396 times; we just do not know what aircraft it used.

10. Both `rva` and `plane` have a column called `year`, and they mean different things:
the year of the flight and the year the aircraft was built. Take the left join from
the previous question, add `suffix="_plane"` to the join, and then compute a new column
`age` equal to `2019 - c.year_plane`. Group by carrier and compute the mean age, sorted
from oldest to newest.

```{python}
(
    rva
    .join(plane, on=c.tailnum, how="left", suffix="_plane")
    .with_columns(age = 2019 - c.year_plane)
    .group_by(c.carrier)
    .agg(mean_age = c.age.mean())
    .sort(c.mean_age, descending=True)
)
```

After Allegiant's missing value, United (`UA`) flies the oldest aircraft, about 18 years
old on average.

11. Use a semi-join to keep the rows of `airport` whose `faa` code appears as a `dest`
in `rva`.

```{python}
(
    airport
    .join(rva, left_on=c.faa, right_on=c.dest, how="semi")
)
```

This gives the same 22 airports as question 5, but with no columns added from `rva`
and no grouping needed.

12. Now the weather. The weather is recorded once per hour, so the key that connects a
flight to the weather is four columns: `year`, `month`, `day`, and `hour`. Join
`weather` onto `rva` using all four columns, and select the columns `month`, `day`,
`hour`, `dep_delay`, and `wind_speed`.

```{python}
(
    rva
    .join(weather, on=[c.year, c.month, c.day, c.hour])
    .select(c.month, c.day, c.hour, c.dep_delay, c.wind_speed)
)
```

This is the same kind of key that you will use in your project to join your `hours`
table to the weather: a date and an hour, together.

13. Take the join from the previous question and add a column `windy` that is true when
`wind_speed` is at least 20. Then group by `windy` and compute the number of flights and
the mean departure delay.

```{python}
(
    rva
    .join(weather, on=[c.year, c.month, c.day, c.hour])
    .with_columns(windy = c.wind_speed >= 20)
    .group_by(c.windy)
    .agg(
        n = pl.len(),
        mean_dep_delay = c.dep_delay.mean()
    )
)
```

Only 279 flights left in winds of 20 miles per hour or more, but they were about 24
minutes late on average, compared with 10 minutes for the rest. The `null` group is the
hours where the wind speed was not recorded.

14. Add a column `carrier_mean` to `rva` giving the mean departure delay of each
flight's carrier. Use `.over()`, and select `carrier`, `dep_delay`, and `carrier_mean`.

```{python}
(
    rva
    .with_columns(carrier_mean = c.dep_delay.mean().over(c.carrier))
    .select(c.carrier, c.dep_delay, c.carrier_mean)
)
```

15. Now get the same column a second way. Inside the join, build a small table with
one row per carrier using `.group_by()` and `.agg()`, and join it onto `rva` by
`carrier`. Select the same three columns.

```{python}
(
    rva
    .join(
        rva.group_by(c.carrier).agg(carrier_mean = c.dep_delay.mean()),
        on=c.carrier
    )
    .select(c.carrier, c.dep_delay, c.carrier_mean)
)
```

The numbers are the same as in the previous question. `.over()` is shorter, but the
second approach works even when the summary comes from a different table.

16. Last one. Build a table with one row per day, joining a summary of the flights to a
summary of the weather. Group `rva` by `year`, `month`, and `day` and compute the mean
departure delay; inside the join, group `weather` the same way and compute the mean
visibility. Draw a scatter plot of the mean delay against the mean visibility.

```{python}
(
    rva
    .group_by(c.year, c.month, c.day)
    .agg(mean_dep_delay = c.dep_delay.mean())
    .join(
        weather.group_by(c.year, c.month, c.day).agg(mean_visib = c.visib.mean()),
        on=[c.year, c.month, c.day]
    )
    .ggplot(aes(c.mean_visib, c.mean_dep_delay))
    .geom_point()
)
```

Most days have a mean visibility of exactly 10 miles, and those days range from early
to more than 40 minutes late. A day's average visibility explains very little about
how late Richmond's flights ran.
